extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and worldbuilders (especially speculative fiction authors) interested in using food effectively in story and worldbuilding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for integrating food into fiction as a worldbuilding and character-building tool: what to show, what to avoid, and how to root food in culture, history, production, and sensory memory. Includes a writing homework prompt to create a fictional meal with provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food must matter to a character
rubrics_metrics.description: When food appears in fiction, it should matter to a character — whether as a good memory or a bad one — and the narrative should explain why it matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not just what’s in the dish: show what about the cooking, whether it’s a communal effort, whether it’s for a particular purpose, and how it ties to the character’s memories and identity. Example: Sophie sharing an 'untraditional meal' as an amalgamation of comfort foods; reviewers responded because the food mattered to the character and had social meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions must be nourishing and purposeful (avoid 'intestine stuffing')
rubrics_metrics.description: Food descriptions should 'nourish' the narrative — serve a purpose beyond sensory adornment — not be merely filler or 'intestine stuffing' (hash ris and thron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the food scene provides character insight, advances theme, or contributes to worldbuilding; avoid verbose gratuitous food description that doesn't serve the story. The transcript warns against descriptions that are merely 'adequate' and do not provide narrative nourishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the ubiquitous feast-or-stew cliché
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic fantasy often falls into two food tropes: enormous feasts or a ubiquitous, generic stew. This is a missed opportunity for nuanced worldbuilding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary depiction of meals; avoid relying on a single broad trope. Use specific dishes, rituals, and contexts instead of fallback 'feast' or 'we ate stew' shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make food reveal the world (provenance, production, class, scarcity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meals should tell us something about the world: where ingredients come from, who produces them, class differences, and how scarcity or abundance shapes culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use food to indicate sea exploration (e.g., presence of New World crops like potatoes), wealth (banquets), food insecurity (meals of opportunity), agricultural suitability (cattle vs. crops), and connections to empire/colonialism. Consider how production, distribution, and environment shape diet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch historical/anachronistic accuracy of ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: Ingredients carry historical and geographic implications; including anachronistic or out-of-place ingredients signals technologies, trade, or exploration that must be accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: potatoes in a medieval-European-type setting imply sea exploration and contact with the New World. Be deliberate: if an ingredient exists, the world should support how it got there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show preparation and ritual (preparation → presentation → consumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ritual of food — the way it is prepared, presented, and consumed — conveys meaning and character, and can be an effective locus for scene work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail communal cooking, special preparations, timing (Saturday prep for Sunday breakfast), and who participates. Ritual signals culture and creates memorable, character-building moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use food as metaphor and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Food scenes can encode potent metaphors and anchor sensory memories that reveal emotional states and narrative transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: toasted bread and butter and jam representing moving from cold gray darkness to warm golden light. Link sensory detail to emotional beats to make food scenes resonate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for practical/logistical realism (cooking time, diet biology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical realities — how long something takes to cook, what resources are available while traveling, and biological effects of diets — should be considered so food scenes remain plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include characters making hours-long stews while on the road or relying on only lean meats (rabbit starvation). Use such facts to inform believable choices or to deliberately subvert expectations with explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think through food production and environmental logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide why certain foodways exist in a place based on environment, technology, and economy (e.g., arid lands favor livestock over crops).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider agricultural limits, animal husbandry, trade networks, and food standards. The hosts recommend resources (e.g., Dr. Sarah Taber, Farm to Taber) to deepen realistic worldbuilding about production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make future foods culturally rooted and palatable
rubrics_metrics.description: In science fiction, avoid defaulting to bland mushes or pills; instead root future food in the cultures and circumstances of those who eat it so it feels meaningful and edible to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of good practice: The Expanse, which invents distinctive cuisines (Martian, Belter) and language; avoid one-dimensional future-food tropes and imagine how diverse cultures would adapt food for space environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting alien/other cuisines only as repulsive horror
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't make alien or nonhuman food merely grotesque to signal 'otherness'; instead show cross-cultural appreciation and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexample: Klingon food often played as horror; better is Deep Space Nine's scene where Klingon food is shared and enjoyed, showing cultural exchange rather than pure revulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider immigrant/time-locked cuisines
rubrics_metrics.description: Immigrant cuisines can be 'time-locked' to the moment of migration; different waves of immigration yield different flavors and food traditions that diverge from the homeland's present cuisine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to create layered, believable food cultures — e.g., 'New York Korean' vs contemporary Korea — and to signal migration history and generational change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show sharing (or withholding) of home food as social signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a character shares their home cooking — or avoids sharing it for fear of judgment — reveals social belonging, embarrassment, and identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: characters embarrassed to bring pungent foods to school/work; sharing an 'untraditional' comfort meal with friends as an act of identity and connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meals should serve a narrative purpose beyond eating
rubrics_metrics.description: A meal scene should contribute to plot, character development, theme, or worldbuilding rather than being mere 'we ate' filler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose could be plot mechanics (ideally) or character/world detail. If the meal has no narrative function, consider cutting or reworking it to make it meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework: invent a fictional meal with history and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise prompt: imagine a fictional meal in a fantasy or science-fiction world; describe its history, provenance, cultural origins, ingredient sources, and what it means to the family eating it, then write a short scene tracking its preparation and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate cultural availability, trade, immigration/time-locking, and character significance into the scene; explicitly work production, provenance, and social meaning into the story.
